ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & UT Inspection in Atlanta, GA
ut.description: On-site ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection for Atlanta tanks, boilers, piping and structural steel. Request a quote from Atlantis NDT.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Atlanta, Georgia
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out ultrasonic testing (UT) in Atlanta, Georgia: wall-thickness surveys on storage tanks, boilers, pressure vessels and process piping, and shear-wave examination of structural and pressure-retaining welds. Technicians travel to your plant, terminal, airport facility or construction site for the agreed scope and report against the code you name. Send the component, material, thickness range and governing code, and request a UT quote for Atlanta. We reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Atlanta

Atlanta is a distribution, transportation and construction city rather than a refining city, and that shapes the UT work. Refined fuel reaches the metro area through interstate pipelines and is held in tank terminals, so aboveground storage tanks and their nozzles are a steady source of thickness work. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport and the logistics parks around it run fuel hydrant piping, ground support equipment and large steel-framed buildings. Rail yards and intermodal terminals add crane rails, car-handling equipment and tank-car loading racks.

Inside the perimeter, campus and hospital steam plants, district chilled-water loops, data center cooling systems and food and beverage plants with ammonia refrigeration all depend on carbon steel piping and vessels that lose wall slowly. The Chattahoochee watershed supplies water and wastewater plants with clarifiers, pump casings and buried-then-exposed piping. A steady building boom keeps structural steel fabricators busy with thick-plate groove welds. Each of these has a different UT question, and we scope the examination to that question instead of applying one routine everywhere.

What UT finds and what it misses

Ultrasonic testing sends sound into the metal and listens for the echo. On a corroded wall the echo from the back surface tells you how much steel is left. On a weld, a sound beam launched at an angle reflects from planar flaws such as lack of fusion, incomplete penetration and cracks, and from slag that lies across the beam path. UT works on any metal that transmits sound, magnetic or not, and it sees below the surface, which neither magnetic particle nor penetrant testing can do.

It has limits that the plan has to respect. The surface must be clean enough for couplant to pass sound into the part. Heavy scale, flaking paint and deep pitting scatter the signal and can hide a thin spot. Coarse-grained castings and austenitic stainless welds attenuate and redirect the beam, which makes interpretation harder and sometimes impractical with conventional probes. A flaw lying parallel to the beam may return nothing. A procedure written for the real material and geometry is the control for all of these, and where UT is the wrong tool we say so before the work starts.

Thickness surveys on tanks, vessels and piping

Most Atlanta UT jobs start as thickness measurement. The technician marks a grid or a set of condition monitoring locations (CMLs) on the shell, head or pipe, cleans each point, and reads the remaining wall with a dual-element probe, which handles rough and corroded surfaces better than a single-element probe. The instrument is calibrated on a step block of the same material before the survey and checked again during it, and the readings are logged against the location number so next year's survey lines up with this year's.

Where a thin or pitted wall could fool a digital gauge into doubling the reading, the technician switches to an A-scan display and judges the echo directly. Hot service needs a high-temperature probe and couplant plus a temperature correction. The practice behind these readings is ASTM E797 and, for the ASME Section V route, the thickness measurement article in Article 23 (SE-797). Our guide to ultrasonic thickness requirements explains the Section V side in plain terms.

Weld examination with angle-beam shear wave

For groove welds in plate, pipe and structural members, the technician uses angle-beam probes, commonly 45, 60 and 70 degrees, on a wedge that fits the surface. A reference level or distance-amplitude curve is built from side-drilled holes in a calibration block of matching material and thickness, so every signal can be compared with a known reflector. The scan covers the weld and heat-affected zone from both sides where access allows, and each indication is located, sized by amplitude and length, and compared with the acceptance table.

Georgia's steel construction work follows AWS D1.1, which has its own ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, and ASME Section V Article 4 gives the technique for pressure work. UT on welds does not replace visual examination of the cap, and it is not a surface method: toe cracks and surface porosity are found faster by magnetic particle testing in Atlanta or penetrant testing in Atlanta. Many jobs pair UT for the volume with one of those for the surface.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Atlanta work

The code that governs the item sets the technique and the acceptance limits; the UT procedure only carries them out. For aboveground storage tanks the in-service rules are API 653, with thickness data feeding the tank's remaining life and next-inspection date. Pressure vessels fall under API 510 for in-service inspection and ASME Section VIII Division 1 for construction, whose Appendix 12 covers ultrasonic examination of welds. Process piping follows API 570 in service and ASME B31.3 for new work, where paragraph 344.6 describes ultrasonic examination and Table 341.3.2 holds the acceptance criteria.

Under API 510, 570 and 653 the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection. Our part is the examination itself: calibrated readings, indications and a clean data set the inspector can use. For structural steel the reference is AWS D1.1, for bridge steel AWS D1.5, and for contact UT of weldments ASTM E164. Where the contract names an edition, the procedure is written to that edition, not to the newest one.

Georgia boiler and pressure vessel rules

Georgia regulates boilers and pressure vessels through the Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, which inspects them and issues certificates of authority to companies that install or service them; the detailed rules sit in chapter 120-3-26 of the state's rules and regulations. The National Board Inspection Code governs repairs and alterations. In practice that means a thickness survey on a steam boiler, an air receiver or an ammonia vessel in an Atlanta building often feeds a state or insurer inspection, and the owner needs readings that an inspector can accept.

For process plants with covered chemicals, OSHA's process safety management rule, 29 CFR 1910.119, requires mechanical integrity: inspection and testing of pressure vessels, tanks and piping to recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice. Ammonia refrigeration above the threshold quantity falls under it, and it is a common reason Atlanta cold-storage and food plants schedule piping thickness work.

Who does the examination

Atlantis has no office in Atlanta. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope. They are qualified under the company's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A: a Level II technician sets up and calibrates the equipment, performs the examination and interprets the results, while an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the reports. The Level III on our side is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Under SNT-TC-1A it is the employer that certifies its personnel, which is why the written practice is part of the paperwork and not an afterthought.

If your own program needs a written practice or a procedure written to a specific code edition, our Level III consulting and written practice development pages describe how that work is done.

What the UT report contains

A usable UT report lets someone who was not on site understand exactly what was measured. Ours identifies the component and its location in the facility, the procedure and revision, the instrument, probe and calibration block, the calibration checks, and the technician and certification level. Thickness work includes a grid or CML sketch with every reading, the nominal and minimum required wall, and the lowest reading found. Weld work lists each indication with position along the weld, depth, length, amplitude against the reference level, and an accept or reject decision against the named criteria. Limitations, such as an area that could not be scanned because of an attachment, are written down, not left for you to discover.

Planning a UT job in Atlanta

Several local realities decide how smoothly an Atlanta job runs. Summer heat and sun can push steel surfaces well above ordinary couplant limits, so tank shells and roof-level piping are often read in the morning shade or with high-temperature couplant. Spring brings heavy pollen and red clay dust that clog couplant and need wiping before every reading. Winter nights drop near freezing only occasionally, but water-based couplant can stiffen on cold steel, and the procedure should say what to use. Thunderstorm season interrupts outdoor tank work, so build slack into schedules.

Access matters as much as weather. Airside work at the airport needs facility-arranged security badging and escorts. Interstate traffic around the perimeter makes arrival time unpredictable, so agree start times with the site contact and do not plan back-to-back locations on a tight clock. Plants will want safety orientation, lockout and permit requirements explained before the crew arrives. Scaffolding, insulation removal and cleaning are normally the owner's tasks, and a single sentence in the quote about who provides them avoids most disputes.

UT, MT or PT for your Atlanta job

Choose the method by the question. If you need to know how much wall remains, or whether a weld has an internal flaw, UT is the method. If the concern is a surface crack in carbon steel, such as a toe crack or a fatigue crack at a lug, use magnetic particle testing. If the material is stainless or aluminum, or the question is whether a ground-out area is crack-free, penetrant testing is the choice. Many fabrication and repair jobs use more than one: UT for the volume and MT or PT for the surface. Our comparison of MT and PT helps with that decision, and the national UT service page shows the full scope.

Training your own UT technicians

Some Atlanta employers prefer to qualify their own staff. Atlantis trains technicians in UT Level 1 and UT Level 2, with practice on the Practical NDT ultrasonic simulator, and the NDT training page for Atlanta explains how the theory, simulator and hands-on parts fit together under your employer's written practice. The SNT-TC-1A eligibility checker shows the experience hours a candidate needs.

faq.q: What does ultrasonic testing cost to schedule in Atlanta?
faq.a: The scope drives the quote: number of thickness points, weld length and thickness, access, scaffolding, and travel. Send the component list or drawings through the quote link and we will scope the work and reply within one business day.

faq.q: Can UT measure wall thickness through paint or coating in Atlanta?
faq.a: Often yes. Many gauges can read through a sound, well-bonded coating if the procedure allows it and the calibration accounts for it. Flaking, blistered or thick coatings scatter the signal, so the technician may need to remove them locally and read bare metal.

faq.q: Does Atlantis inspect Atlanta storage tanks for API 653?
faq.a: We perform the ultrasonic thickness work on tank shells, floors where reachable, roofs and nozzles and deliver the data. Under API 653 the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection, and uses our data to set the corrosion rate and remaining life.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on a weld in Georgia?
faq.a: That depends on the construction code for the weld and on what the owner will accept. Some codes include ultrasonic examination provisions for production welds and others do not. The substitution is agreed with the owner, the engineer and any authorized inspector before the work starts.

faq.q: How hot can a surface be for UT thickness readings?
faq.a: Standard probes and couplants have modest temperature limits, but high-temperature probes and couplants extend the range considerably. The procedure states the limit and any correction. For very hot lines, readings may be taken after the line is shut down.

faq.q: What do I need to prepare before UT technicians arrive in Atlanta?
faq.a: Provide safe access, scaffolding or lifts where needed, removal of insulation at test points, a clean contact surface, drawings or CML maps, the applicable code edition, and site orientation requirements. A short call before mobilization confirms who provides what.

faq.q: Which codes does an Atlanta UT weld inspection follow?
faq.a: The code on the drawing decides: AWS D1.1 for structural steel, AWS D1.5 for bridge steel, ASME Section VIII and B31.3 for pressure equipment and piping, and API 1104 for pipeline girth welds. The UT procedure is written to that code and edition.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Atlanta?
faq.a: No. Technicians are mobilized from outside the city to your site for the agreed scope. We tell you in the quote what travel the job needs, and all procedures, reports and Level III review are handled the same way as for any other site.

faq.q: Can my own technicians learn UT through Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers UT Level 1 and Level 2 training with a simulator for practice. Qualification and certification are done by the employer under its written practice, so the course supports that process and does not replace it.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Atlanta, GA | MPI
mt.description: On-site mag particle testing of welds, lifting lugs, cranes and structural steel in Atlanta, Georgia. Wet fluorescent and dry yoke MPI. Request a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Atlanta, Georgia
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs magnetic particle inspection (MPI, also called mag particle testing or MT) on carbon and low-alloy steel in Atlanta, Georgia. Typical work is weld toes and fillets on structural steel, lifting lugs and rigging points, crane and equipment frames, pressure vessel attachment welds and ground-out repair areas. Technicians travel to your site with yokes and particle materials for the agreed scope. Request an MT quote for Atlanta with the component, material and governing code, and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle testing is used in Atlanta

Metro Atlanta has a great deal of fabricated carbon steel that carries load, and that is where MT earns its place. A long run of commercial construction keeps structural steel shops and erectors busy, and every complete-penetration weld and connection with a fatigue or brittle-fracture concern is a candidate for a surface check. Heavy lifting is part of daily life here: tower cranes on building sites, bridge and gantry cranes in warehouses and rail terminals, and the hooks, shackles and pins that go with them.

The airport district adds ground support equipment frames, tug and loader structures, and the steel that carries jet bridges. Rail yards generate repair welding on car and locomotive components that regularly returns to the shop for a crack check. Film and event production, a large local industry, relies on rigging steel, truss and lifting hardware that needs periodic crack inspection before it goes overhead. Fuel terminals and process plants supply the pressure side: nozzle-to-shell welds, support lugs and repair welds on carbon steel vessels and tanks.

What MT finds and what it misses

MT works because a crack interrupts the magnetic field in a ferromagnetic part and spills flux into the air. Fine iron particles gather at that leakage and draw a visible line on the surface. It finds surface-breaking cracks, laps, seams and lack of fusion, and it finds discontinuities lying just under the surface, usually to a shallow depth. It is fast, it shows the flaw directly on the part, and it works through thin non-magnetic coatings within limits set by the procedure.

The method has hard boundaries. The material must be ferromagnetic: carbon and low-alloy steels qualify, while austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper and titanium do not, and for those you need penetrant testing. MT does not see flaws deep in the wall, so it does not replace UT for a thickness survey or a volumetric weld examination. A crack running along the field lines produces little leakage, which is why the field must be applied in two directions. Heavy scale, grease and thick paint reduce sensitivity and must be removed in the examination area.

Technique: yokes, particles and field direction

On most field work the tool is an electromagnetic yoke. The technician sets the pole spacing, checks that the yoke can lift the required test weight (at least 10 pounds for an AC yoke and at least 40 pounds for a DC or permanent-magnet yoke, per ASME Section V Article 7) and magnetizes the area between the legs. The yoke is then turned about ninety degrees and the area is examined again, so cracks in any direction are caught. Prods can magnetize larger areas but burn the surface if they arc, so they are limited by procedure and normally avoided on finished or critical surfaces.

Dry visible particles in a contrasting color suit rough weld surfaces in warm, dry conditions; wet particles in a liquid vehicle give higher sensitivity on smoother parts and on fatigue-critical details. Fluorescent particles are examined under UV-A light in a darkened area, which outdoors in Atlanta usually means a tent or shroud. A field indicator or other flux-direction check proves that the field is strong enough and aimed correctly before indications are accepted. Where residual magnetism would interfere with later welding, machining or service, the part is demagnetized and checked.

Surface condition and coatings before MT

Most poor MT results trace back to the surface. On a structural weld the cap must be free of loose slag, spatter and heavy ripple, because the particles collect at every sharp feature and bury the real indication. Oil and grease make dry powder clump and wet particles streak. Rust and mill scale lift the yoke legs off the metal and weaken the field. Where a coating stays on, the technician checks its thickness against the procedure's limit and confirms with a known artificial flaw or a field indicator that sensitivity has survived.

In Atlanta, galvanized members and shop-primed steel are common on building frames, and each has its own quirks. Zinc is non-magnetic but thin enough on most members to pass the field. Primer applied heavily over a weld toe may not. The cleaning method, usually wire brushing, grinding or solvent wiping, is written into the procedure so a crew arriving at an erected frame knows what to do before a yoke is switched on, and so the report can show what was done.

Reading indications: relevant, non-relevant and false

Particles build up for more than one reason, and the technician has to sort them. A relevant indication comes from a real discontinuity such as a crack or lack of fusion. A non-relevant indication is caused by something real but harmless, such as a sharp change of section, a keyway, or the edge of a weld where the geometry itself leaks flux. A false indication has no metallurgical cause at all: particles stuck in a scratch, a streak of excess particles, or magnetic writing from contact with another magnet.

The technician re-examines a suspect area after light cleaning and re-magnetizing, and a crack-like line that returns in the same place after the area is demagnetized and wiped is treated as real. Linear indications are measured and compared with the code's limits, which are tighter for linear than for rounded ones. Grinding to remove a crack is followed by a new examination with the same procedure, so the final record shows the flaw gone, not just ground.

Codes and acceptance criteria for MT in Georgia

MT is written to the code that governs the part. ASME Section V Article 7 sets the technique, and ASTM E709 and E1444 are the guide and practice behind it. For pressure vessels built to ASME Section VIII Division 1, Appendix 6 gives the MT method and acceptance limits; for process piping ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 calls for magnetic particle examination and Table 341.3.2 holds the acceptance criteria. Structural welds follow AWS D1.1, and bridge steel built under the state department of transportation follows AWS D1.5.

Acceptance is a judgment against specific limits, not a hunt for any particle. Round indications, linear indications and their spacing are classified by size, and relevant indications are separated from false ones caused by changes in section, magnetic writing or surface roughness. For in-service tanks, vessels and piping, API 653, 510 and 570 leave the inspection decision with the owner's authorized inspector, and our MT results are the data that inspector reviews.

Who performs and reviews the work

We do not keep an office in Atlanta. Technicians are mobilized to your location for the agreed scope and work under the company's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician sets up the equipment, performs the examination and interprets the indications; an ASNT Level III writes and approves the procedure and reviews the report. On Atlanta jobs the approving Level III is Anoop Rayavarapu, who holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. The employer certifies its own personnel under SNT-TC-1A, so the written practice and the individual records stay in the file with the report.

For fabricators building their own program, written practice development and outsourced Level III consulting are available as separate services.

What the MT report contains

The report names the component, its identification and its position in the structure, the procedure number and revision, the method and technique (yoke, prods or bench), the particle type and vehicle, the lighting measurement for the examination, and the yoke lift test or field verification. It states the technician, certification level and date. Each indication is recorded with location, orientation and length, and given an accept or reject decision against the stated code table. Sketches or photographs mark the areas examined, and any area that could not be examined because of access or geometry is listed as a limitation. Repairs and re-examinations are tied back to the original indication number.

Planning an MT job in Atlanta

Atlanta's weather affects MT more than people expect. Summer sun can heat dark steel well past the range where wet particles behave properly and dry powder clings unevenly, so inspection is often scheduled for early morning or shaded areas. Humid air can leave dew on steel that is cooler than the surrounding air, which ruins particle mobility until it is dried. Spring pollen and red clay dust settle on freshly cleaned surfaces and read as false indications under UV light if the area is not wiped just before examination.

Fluorescent work in daylight needs shelter, and thunderstorms in the warm season shut down open-air jobs quickly. Crane and rigging inspections on active building sites depend on the general contractor's lift schedule and permit system. Airside and rail-yard work needs facility security arrangements. Because crews travel to Atlanta, grouping several components into a single visit saves cost and avoids repeated mobilization, and a pre-job call about surface condition and access usually removes most surprises.

MT, PT or UT for your Atlanta job

Use MT when the part is steel and the worry is a surface or near-surface crack. Use penetrant testing in Atlanta when the material is stainless steel or aluminum, or when MT is impractical because of geometry or coating. Use ultrasonic testing in Atlanta when the question concerns wall thickness or a flaw inside a weld. Our complete guide to magnetic particle testing and the national MT service page go deeper into technique and scope.

Training your own MT technicians

Employers who want their own qualified staff can send people through MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training. The NDT training page for Atlanta explains how the course sits alongside the employer's written practice, and the Article 7 explainer is a good primer before the course starts.

faq.q: What is magnetic particle inspection used for in Atlanta?
faq.a: In Atlanta it is mainly used on structural steel welds, crane and rigging hardware, equipment frames, and attachment welds on carbon steel tanks and vessels. It shows surface and near-surface cracks that visual examination can miss, and it does so directly on the part.

faq.q: Can MT be done on stainless steel or aluminum?
faq.a: Not with the magnetic particle method, because those materials are not ferromagnetic and do not hold the field the particles depend on. Penetrant testing is the usual surface method for austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and titanium.

faq.q: Does the paint have to come off before MT?
faq.a: Not always. A thin, sound, non-magnetic coating can stay if the procedure allows it and the sensitivity is demonstrated. Loose paint, scale, rust and heavy build must be removed from the examination area, and the coating condition is noted in the report.

faq.q: Is wet fluorescent MT better than dry powder?
faq.a: Wet fluorescent particles are more sensitive to fine cracks and suit smoother, fatigue-critical parts, while dry visible powder is practical on rough weld surfaces in the field. The procedure and the code decide which is acceptable for your component.

faq.q: How are cracks in every direction detected with a yoke?
faq.a: The area is magnetized, examined, and then magnetized again with the yoke turned roughly ninety degrees, so a crack that lies along the first field is crossed by the second. Both passes are required by the technique, and both are recorded.

faq.q: Do parts need demagnetizing after MT?
faq.a: Sometimes. If residual magnetism could disturb welding, machining, instruments or moving parts, the part is demagnetized and measured. The procedure states when it is required, and the result is noted in the report so the next trade knows the part is clean.

faq.q: Does MT meet ASME and AWS requirements?
faq.a: It can, when the procedure is written to the code in force. ASME Section V Article 7, Section VIII Appendix 6, ASME B31.3 and AWS D1.1 each define how the examination is done and what is acceptable, and the report cites the edition used.

faq.q: Does Atlantis keep a crew in Atlanta?
faq.a: No. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, with equipment calibrated and procedures approved by a Level III. We confirm travel details in the quote and agree who provides access, power and surface preparation before the visit.

faq.q: Can my team be trained in magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers MT Level 1 and Level 2 courses and a practice route through the simulator and practice tests. Certification is awarded by the employer under its written practice, so training is one part of the qualification record.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing & Dye Penetrant in Atlanta, GA
pt.description: On-site dye penetrant inspection (PT) of stainless, aluminum and steel welds and castings in Atlanta, Georgia. Visible and fluorescent PT. Request a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Atlanta, Georgia
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs liquid penetrant testing, also called dye penetrant inspection or PT, in Atlanta, Georgia. PT finds cracks and porosity that are open to the surface of welds, castings, forgings and machined parts, in stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and carbon steel alike. Technicians travel to your plant, shop or job site with penetrant materials and a written procedure for the agreed scope. Request a PT quote for Atlanta with the material, surface condition and governing code, and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in Atlanta

Penetrant testing fits the materials that magnetic particle testing cannot handle, and metro Atlanta has plenty of them. Food, beverage and dairy processing plants build with stainless steel piping and tanks, and their sanitary welds must be free of surface-breaking cracks and pits where product can lodge. Data center and hospital mechanical rooms use stainless and copper-nickel components and aluminum ductwork and frames. The airport district maintains aluminum ground support equipment, stair trucks and fuel servicing equipment where welded cracks are a routine repair item.

Fabrication shops serving the construction boom weld aluminum railings, stainless architectural steel and curtain-wall supports and often want a crack check on the root or final pass. Water and wastewater plants along the river system have stainless and bronze pump parts and valve bodies. Castings and forgings from regional foundries and machine shops are another steady source of work, since the penetrant method shows laps, cold shuts and shrinkage that break the surface.

What PT finds and what it misses

Penetrant is a low-viscosity liquid that enters surface-breaking discontinuities by capillary action. After the excess is removed and a developer applied, the liquid bleeds back out and draws a bright line or dot where the flaw is. PT detects only flaws open to the surface, and it works on almost any non-porous material regardless of magnetism or shape. It shows linear cracks, porosity, laps and seams clearly and gives a direct, photographable result.

It will not see anything below the surface, and it cannot tell you wall thickness. A flaw that has been smeared closed by grinding, shot peening, machining or wire brushing may not take up penetrant, which is why cleaning and etching rules matter. Porous surfaces, rough weld ripples and heavy oxide can trap penetrant and create false indications. Contaminants such as oil, paint and rust block the liquid from entering a crack, so the surface preparation steps in the procedure are part of the method, not an extra.

Technique: penetrant types, dwell and development

The technician starts with cleaning: degrease, remove scale and paint in the examination area, and let solvent evaporate fully. Penetrant is then applied by spray, brush or immersion and left to dwell for a time set by the procedure, which depends on the material, the type of discontinuity looked for and the temperature. Excess penetrant is removed in a way that depends on the system: solvent-removable systems are wiped with a cloth lightly dampened with cleaner, water-washable systems are rinsed, and post-emulsified systems use an emulsifier step.

Developer is applied in a thin, even coat, and the part is examined during and after the development time. Visible-dye systems are viewed in white light with a defined minimum intensity, while fluorescent systems are viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area, which gives higher sensitivity for fine cracks. Indications are evaluated against the acceptance criteria, and the area is post-cleaned afterward, especially where residue could affect later welding or service in stainless piping.

Cleaning, etching and the over-removal problem

Penetrant testing is only as good as the first five minutes of preparation. Grinding, buffing, shot blasting and wire brushing can smear metal across a crack mouth and close it to penetrant, so on machined, ground or blasted surfaces the procedure may require a light etch before inspection. Aluminum and stainless castings with machined faces are common examples. Oil from cutting fluid, residue from earlier penetrant tests and old paint all block capillary entry, and each needs its own removal step.

The opposite mistake happens at the removal step. If the technician wipes or rinses too hard, penetrant is pulled out of shallow cracks and the indication disappears. Solvent should be applied to the cloth, not sprayed directly on the surface, and water-washable systems need controlled pressure and time. These details are why a trained Level II matters more on PT than the simple appearance of the method suggests, and why the report records the removal method as well as the materials.

Reading indications and judging them against the code

Indications appear within seconds as penetrant bleeds into the developer, and the technician watches the surface during development because fine cracks show early and then spread. A sharp, thin red or fluorescent line points to a crack, a row of dots to porosity or a tight linear flaw, and a broad stain to a rough surface or poor removal. The examination is repeated if the result is unclear, and the area is cleaned and re-tested from scratch instead of re-developing the same surface.

Relevant indications are measured and compared with the code's limits for length, type and spacing. A crack, in any size, is rejected by nearly every construction code, while rounded indications are allowed up to stated size and density. The record notes the code table used, so a reader can see whether an accepted indication was close to the limit and plan the next inspection accordingly.

Codes and acceptance criteria for PT in Georgia

ASME Section V Article 6 defines how the examination is done, and ASTM E165 is the general-industry practice. Section VIII Division 1 gives PT methods and acceptance in Appendix 8, and ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 calls for liquid penetrant examination on process piping with acceptance limits in Table 341.3.2. AWS D1.1 permits PT as an alternative to MT for some structural welds, and AWS D1.6 covers stainless structural welding. Contract documents may add owner requirements, including limits on halogen and sulfur in penetrant materials used on stainless and nickel alloys, and the procedure should state them.

For in-service vessels and piping the authorized inspector decides under API 510 and 570, and our PT data supports that decision. Georgia boiler and pressure vessel work also touches the state's inspection program run by the Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, so repairs on registered equipment need records an inspector can read without a call.

Who performs and reviews the work

Atlantis does not maintain an office in Atlanta. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the scope you approve. They work under the company's written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A: a Level II technician carries out and interprets the PT, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. That Level III is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Certification of individual technicians is done by the employer, which is the reason our records show the written practice reference and the technician's level on every report.

Typical PT scopes we scope for Atlanta customers

A few scope patterns come up repeatedly. One is a weld-by-weld check of stainless process piping before a food or beverage line is commissioned, usually at the root pass and again on the finished weld. Another is a crack check on a repaired aluminum frame, stair or loader structure after the repair weld is dressed. A third is acceptance inspection of machined castings and valve bodies on receipt, where a quick penetrant check on sealing faces and fillets catches flaws before assembly. Finally, there are post-repair checks after grinding out a defect found by another method, to prove the cavity is clean before it is welded.

What the PT report contains

A PT report records the component and location, the procedure and revision, and the penetrant system with manufacturer, type, method and the batch or lot numbers of penetrant, remover and developer. It lists the surface temperature, cleaning method, dwell time, developer time and light intensity, plus the technician and level. Indications are described by type (linear or rounded), location and length, with a photograph where possible, and each is marked accept or reject against the cited criteria. Areas not examined and the reason are stated. Re-examination after repair uses the same procedure and is cross-referenced to the first report.

Planning a PT job in Atlanta

The key planning limit for PT is temperature. The standard temperature window in Article 6 of ASME Section V runs from 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit, for the part and the penetrant materials alike, and outside it the procedure must be qualified at the temperature actually met on the job. Atlanta summers can push sun-exposed steel and aluminum past 125 degrees, so outdoor work is often done early or in shade, and surfaces are cooled before penetrant goes on. The occasional winter morning near freezing creates the opposite problem, with penetrant thickening and dwell times stretching.

Humidity and rain affect cleaning and drying, and spring pollen can settle on a prepared surface in minutes and get picked up as false indications. Fluorescent work in daylight needs a darkened enclosure. Because crews travel to Atlanta, check that solvents, rags and waste disposal are acceptable to the plant, that confined-space or hot-work permits are arranged, and that stainless components have not been exposed to chloride-bearing cleaners the specification forbids. A short pre-job call about materials, finish and access usually settles these points.

PT, MT or UT for your Atlanta job

Choose PT for surface cracks in non-magnetic metals, for fine cracks in ground or machined surfaces, and for checking a repair area on any material. Choose magnetic particle testing in Atlanta when the part is steel and speed matters, and ultrasonic testing in Atlanta when the issue is below the surface or concerns wall thickness. The MT versus PT comparison sets the trade-offs out, and the national penetrant testing page describes the full service.

Training your own PT technicians

Teams that want in-house PT capability can take PT Level 1 and PT Level 2 training, and practice on the Practical NDT penetrant simulator. The NDT training page for Atlanta explains how the course, practical and employer certification fit together, and the Article 6 explainer is useful preparation.

faq.q: What can liquid penetrant testing find?
faq.a: It finds cracks, laps, seams, porosity and other discontinuities that are open to the surface. It cannot find flaws below the surface or measure thickness, so it is often paired with ultrasonic testing when the volume of a weld matters too.

faq.q: Which materials can be inspected by PT in Atlanta?
faq.a: Almost any non-porous material: stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys, titanium, copper alloys and carbon steel. That makes it the standard surface method for the stainless and aluminum fabrications common in food plants, airport equipment and architectural metalwork.

faq.q: What temperature limits apply to dye penetrant inspection?
faq.a: Article 6 of ASME Section V gives a normal working window of 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for both the part and the penetrant. Outside that window the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature, which matters on hot Atlanta summer afternoons.

faq.q: Visible dye or fluorescent penetrant: which is used?
faq.a: Visible dye works in white light and suits general field work, while fluorescent penetrant needs UV-A light in a darkened area and is more sensitive to fine cracks. The code, the material and the owner's specification decide which system is used.

faq.q: Why does surface preparation matter so much for PT?
faq.a: Penetrant can only enter a crack that is clean and open. Oil, paint, rust, scale or smeared metal from grinding can block it, so cleaning, and sometimes etching, is a required step. A skipped cleaning step can hide a real defect.

faq.q: Can PT be used on stainless steel without damaging it?
faq.a: Yes, provided the penetrant materials are low in halogens and sulfur when the specification requires it, and the part is post-cleaned afterward. The procedure and the batch certifications for the materials are listed on the report.

faq.q: How are PT indications judged acceptable or not?
faq.a: The relevant code states limits on indication size, type and spacing. Linear indications are held to tighter limits than rounded ones, and false indications from surface features are separated from relevant ones before an accept or reject decision is made.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a team stationed in Atlanta?
faq.a: No. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope and bring the penetrant system, lighting and a Level III approved procedure. Access, power, permits and any surface preparation are agreed in advance and written into the quote.

faq.q: Can my employees learn penetrant testing with Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers PT Level 1 and Level 2 courses with simulator practice and practice questions. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its technicians, so the course supports your written practice and does not replace it.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing (RT) Alternatives in Atlanta, GA
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. See UT as an alternative, Level III radiograph review and RT training for Atlanta, Georgia. Get a quote.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) Options in Atlanta, Georgia
rt.html:
If you searched for radiographic testing in Atlanta, one point comes first. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing on any Atlanta project, or anywhere else in the United States. Industrial radiography here is a licensed activity, controlled under the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's rules in 10 CFR Part 34 or the equivalent rules of an Agreement State, and it is not a service we offer. This page explains what we can do for an Atlanta project that calls for radiographic examination, and where each option fits.

Ultrasonic testing as the volumetric alternative

For many welds, ultrasonic examination finds the same internal flaws that radiography finds, with no radiation and no exclusion zone, which suits busy Atlanta plants, airport facilities and building sites. Ultrasonic testing in Atlanta covers angle-beam weld examination and thickness work. The substitution is not automatic. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, AWS D1.1 has its own acceptance criteria for ultrasonic examination of groove welds, and ASME Section VIII allows ultrasonic examination in place of radiography only under specific conditions.

That is why the change is agreed with the owner, the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector before the job begins. We can help prepare the technical basis, which lists the weld geometry, material, thickness and the code clause relied on, so the decision is documented and not improvised in the field.

ASNT Level III radiograph review without a radiation licence

Reviewing a radiograph needs no source, so it needs no radiation licence. An ASNT Level III from Atlantis reviews film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, gives a second read on disputed indications, and checks that density, sensitivity and image quality indicators meet the requirement. We can also review an RT contractor's procedure and written practice. The Level III is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. The work is done from the records, so travel is rarely needed, and the report sets out what was reviewed and what was found.

This service suits owners who receive radiographs from a contractor and want an independent opinion before accepting a weld, and contractors who want their own procedure checked against the code before a bid. Our Level III consulting page describes how a review engagement is set up.

Surface methods that complement UT and review

Radiography and ultrasonic testing both look through the volume of a weld. Surface cracks and toe flaws are better found by magnetic particle testing in Atlanta for steel and penetrant testing in Atlanta for stainless steel and aluminum. A weld package that pairs UT for the volume with MT or PT for the surface often covers the same ground that radiography plus visual examination would.

RT training and written practice

Technicians who need to understand radiography theory can study it with our RT Level 2 course, which covers the physics, film and image quality, and interpretation against code. Practical exposure work and any radiation safety qualification are arranged by the employer under its licence, and certification is awarded by the employer under its written practice. The NDT training page for Atlanta explains how the pieces fit together, and our written practice development service helps employers set the program up.

How to ask for what you need

Tell us the weld type, material, thickness, the code and edition, and whether the contract requires radiography or only a volumetric method. We will say plainly whether UT is a credible route, whether a radiograph review is what you need, or whether you should go to a licensed radiography contractor. Request a quote for Atlanta and we reply within one business day. Technicians for any field work are mobilized to your site, since Atlantis has no office in Atlanta.

faq.q: Is radiographic testing available through Atlantis in Atlanta?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiography at any US site, Atlanta included. It is a licensed activity under 10 CFR Part 34 or the rules of an Agreement State, and we do not offer it. Instead, the available services are UT, radiograph review and RT training.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing be used instead of RT on my weld?
faq.a: It can be, where the construction code and the owner permit it. Provisions exist in ASME B31.3, API 1104, AWS D1.1 and, under conditions, ASME Section VIII. The change is agreed in advance with the owner, engineer and authorized inspector.

faq.q: Can a Level III review radiographs made by another contractor?
faq.a: Yes. An ASNT Level III can review film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, give a second read on disputed indications, and review the contractor's procedure and written practice.

faq.q: Where can my technicians learn radiographic testing theory?
faq.a: An RT Level 2 course from Atlantis covers theory and interpretation. Practical exposure work and radiation safety qualification are arranged by the employer under its licence, and the employer certifies its own personnel under its written practice.

faq.q: Will you recommend a radiography contractor in Atlanta?
faq.a: No. We do not name or recommend radiography contractors. If your contract requires radiography, choose a contractor that holds the proper licence for your state and verify their credentials and procedure before work starts.
